what_it_does: Many scientific and AI computations work with "sparse" tensors (multi-dimensional arrays of numbers where most entries are zero). Efficient hardware and software for such computations often work in "tiles" — processing one rectangular block of the array at a time — because a tile that fits in the processor's fast on-chip memory (the cache) avoids slow trips to main memory. The right tile size is hard to choose for sparse data, however, because how many nonzero entries end up in a tile depends on the sparsity pattern of the actual data, which changes from one input to the next and is unknown at compile time. This paper takes a probabilistic approach: instead of guessing a fixed tile size, it models the sparsity pattern statistically to predict how a chosen tile size will behave on average, and uses that prediction to select a tile size automatically. The specific details of the probability model are not available from the abstract alone.
